https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c3wj.text: Figure caption, Fears for children's safety in West Bank school as settler attacks rise By Lucy Williamson Middle East correspondent ,Â Reporting from al-Mughayyir, occupied West Bank Published 5 hours ago On the first day of the new Palestinian school year, the head-teacher of al-Mughayyir boys school arrived at work before dawn, walking past the freshly installed barbed wire fencing and reinforced school gates as the sun began creeping through olive trees around the village, deep inside the occupied West Bank. "We are scared," Bassam al Assaf told me. "The students are afraid, and their parents are afraid." Six people, including three pupils at the school, have been killed in al-Mughayyir this year, in a surge of settler-related violence against Palestinians. One of them, 14-year-old Aws al-Naasan, was shot dead by a settler outside the school gates in April. "I was inside my classroom and two little students came rushing to tell me there were settlers close to the school wall," remembers English teacher Waheed Abu Naem, whose brother Jihad was also killed by an Israeli soldier in the same attack. Waheed said he was trying to move pupils to safety inside the school gate when the settler fired towards them. Mobile phone footage shows the moment Aws was shot. "When I turned him onto his back, I saw lots of blood coming from his nose and mouth, and the bullet in his head," said Waheed. "We lost him." He told me that bullets continued hitting the school building, as students hid behind the walls of their classrooms, or lay on the floor. Image caption, English teacher Waheed Abu Naem's brother was killed in a shooting outside the school in April The Israeli military said in a statement at the time that stones had been hurled at a car carrying "civilians including a reservist soldier", and that the reservist had got out of the vehicle and fired at suspects. Israeli media reported the reservist was later suspended from duty and an investigation launched. Since that day, the casualties have grown alongside parents' fears. Over the summer, two more pupils were shot dead by Israeli forces during settler attacks and incursions in the village, along with a 19-year-old who had just left the school. In both cases, Israel's army said its forces responded to instigators of "a violent riot". With three empty desks in the classrooms, some parents were reluctant to send their children back for the new school year. The school sits right on the edge of Al-Mughayyir, an isolated village north-east of Ramallah, increasingly surrounded by Jewish settler outposts, and regularly blocked by Israeli forces who frequently operate an ad-hoc checkpoint at the entrance. Bassam al-Assaf has installed a long barbed-wire fence around the compound and reinforced the school gates, to try and reassure parents. Ambulance crews are now stationed on the road outside, and several parents have volunteered to wait outside the school all day as an extra layer of protection. Image caption, Ambulance crews have been stationed on the road outside the school, while several parents have volunteered to stand outside the gates BBC tracks one week of Israeli settler violence in occupied West Bank Published 28 August Palestinian teens killed during settler attack on West Bank village Published 4 days ago 'We expect our sons to be killed,' father of teen shot dead in West Bank tells BBC Published 3 days ago "I came because it makes the children feel their parents are with them, that they are safe, it gives them a kind of security," said Haroon Bishara, whose boys are in the first and second grades. "We fear for our children more this year," he told me. "We know the situation is not safe at the school." But he said that fear was mixed with a determination not to let the threat from settler attacks force them out. Lined up in the playground for their first assembly, pupils heard the instructions repeated by teachers again and again throughout the day: if soldiers or settlers approach the school, don't shout, don't go near them, don't react. Just over an hour after classes began, settlers were spotted through the school windows: two men, driving sheep through Palestinian fields a couple of hundred metres from the school, as Israeli soldiers stood close by. Minutes later, another settler with a flock of sheep appeared. "They have got closer to the village since April," said Abu Naem. They used to keep their sheep behind this [hill], but now the soldiers bring the settlers up to the village." We asked the Israeli army for its response to all the allegations in this report, but they were unable to provide one before publication. All Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank are illegal under international law. Many of the small ad-hoc settler outposts that have mushroomed around al-Mughayyir are illegal under Israeli law too. But one of the ambulance crews stationed outside the school said that, rather than remove illegal settlements, Israeli soldiers had begun supporting and enabling settler incursions into the village. Hadi al-Naasan, an ambulance driver in the village, said there had been a shift in the behaviour of Israeli forces over the past year. And that the rise in Palestinian deaths and injuries in al-Mughayyir this year reflected that. "At the beginning of 2025, settler attacks were few, due to the army's interventions," he said. "In 2026, the situation changed completely: the settlers became fully protected by the occupation soldiers. This year, the number of martyrs is higher, the number of injuries is also much higher â and the number of child injuries is higher too." Hadi, along with other residents of al-Mughayyir, believes that some Israeli settlers are now deliberately targeting children in order to put pressure on the adults in the village to leave their homes. A UN Commission of Inquiry published in June found that settler attacks "have instrumentalized children , external as part of a broader coercive strategy to drive Palestinians off their land." And it described "a pattern of settlers intentionally targeting Palestinian children" while they were playing near their homes, walking to and from school, tending to farms or herding livestock, "turning everyday spaces into sites of fear". Israel dismissed the report as a "libellous sham". Sheep farmer Sami Abu Rahma firmly believes that some violent settlers are targeting children. At the end of July, his nine-year-old son Salim was shot and injured as he played with his siblings on the family sheep farm outside al-Mughayyir. The bullet is still lodged in his arm. Image caption, Sami's son, Salim, was shot while playing with friends in July Footage from security cameras at the farm shows Salim pointing, and shouting to his parents that settlers are approaching, before running for shelter with his siblings and mother, as two gunshots are heard. Salim is seen grabbing his shoulder. "In that moment, you stop thinking; you just feel fear," Sami told me. "Fear that, God forbid, [the attacker] was shooting to kill. The first thing in your mind is losing the most precious thing you have." The man who shot his son, he said, lived in an illegal settler outpost that appeared next to the farm in June â and had previously shot at Salim in the same area a week before. "You no longer feel you can keep them safe in the street, or even at school," he said. "The settlers don't want us to stay here, [they want us to feel] as if there's no future for us here." Sami said he was the last sheep farmer left in the area, the others all chased away by settler attacks. The settler who shot his son had told the family repeatedly to leave their land, he said. "No matter how determined you might be to stay," he added, "what do you do when settlers start shooting your kids?" The regional settlers council told us that an off-duty soldier was arrested on suspicion of involvement in the shooting. "We regret any harm to innocent people, Jews or Arabs, and oppose any act of violence that violates the law," it said in a statement, adding that it rejected "the attempt to attribute to the entire settlement community in Judea and Samaria acts that have not yet been determined by an investigation, as well as the baseless claim that lawful sheep grazing or Jewish presence in the area are part of a deliberate plan to harm children or drive residents from their homes." Al-Mughayyir is part of a pattern unfolding across the occupied West Bank, with more illegal settler outposts encircling Palestinian villages, more protection for settlers from Israeli forces, and attacks moving from farms and grazing land to built-up areas, where women and children are more at risk. "Children, seeing the army enter, don't grasp the gravity of the situation," said the local ambulance crew, Hadi al-Naasan. "Adults are more aware of how events can unfold." UN figures suggest that the number of Palestinians injured during settler attacks by Israeli soldiers or settlers has risen sharply this year to an average of three injuries per day, and that the number of injuries inflicted directly by settlers themselves is also higher. This rise has been accompanied by an expansion of Israeli settlements and settler outposts in the West Bank. All Israeli settlements in the West Bank are illegal under international law, and Israel's fiercely pro-settlement government is under growing international pressure - including from the UK, which is expected to announce sanctions this week in response to Israeli settlement policies. The arrest of some violent settlers and a reported plan by Israel's prime minister to dismantle illegal outposts in the West Bank have not so far stopped attacks, nor reassured Palestinians who say outposts previously demolished by Israeli authorities were quickly rebuilt. With Israeli elections less than two months away, Israel's Finance Ministry pushed forward plans this week to take over land registration in the West Bank and East Jerusalem, described by the Israeli settlement monitor Peace Now as "a clear step towards annexation". Israel's prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, has attributed settler violence to a tiny extremist minority, describing them in a recent television interview as "150 juvenile delinquents". Since the beginning of 2025, the UN has recorded 316 Palestinians killed by Israeli forces or settlers, and more than 5,600 injured, to the end of July 2026. It says 20 Israelis were killed over the same period, including one child and eight members of the security forces, and 123 Israelis injured. Palestinian parents who have stayed in villages like al-Mughayyir through escalating settler violence are now facing a growing fear of losing their children if they stay on their land. Foreign Home page Foreign 0 0 Azerbaijan’s chairmanship of OTS Member States’ NGO Platform extended 31 August 2026 13:24 (UTC +04:00) An online meeting of country representatives of the Platform of NGOs of the Member States of the Organization of Turkic States was held on August 28, 2026, APA reports. The Platform’s Secretary General, member of the Board of the Azerbaijan National NGO Forum and MP Azer Allahveranov presented a report on the past period, and consultations were held on upcoming tasks. It was noted that the Platform of NGOs of the Member States of the Organization of Turkic States, symbolically established by eight countries in Nakhchivan in November 2025 and headquartered permanently in Baku, has achieved significant success in a short period of time. In this regard, the 2nd Solidarity Forum of NGOs of the OTS Member States, held in Baku in May 2026, was particularly highlighted. It was noted that within the framework of this regional event, held with the Platform as a key partner, cooperation forums of Azerbaijan-Kyrgyzstan, Azerbaijan-Turkmenistan and Azerbaijan-Northern Cyprus NGOs were held for the first time. The work of the Secretariat of the Platform of NGOs of the Member States of the Organization of Turkic States was highly appreciated. Ersin Güzel from Türkiye, Yusuf Tekin from the TRNC, Kairjan Abdykhalykov from Kazakhstan, Ramil Iskandarli from Azerbaijan, Nazgul Joldosheva from Kyrgyzstan, David Biro from Hungary, and other representatives proposed extending the term of office of the Platform’s Secretary General from one year to five years. During the discussions, it was noted that, according to the TURKPA practice, although the rotating chairmanship changes annually among member countries, the Secretary General is elected for a longer term. The proposed initiative was adopted. Secretary General Azer Allahveranov thanked the representatives for their confidence and said that the Platform would further intensify its activities and launch new projects in the coming period. https://www.politico.eu/article/airport-.text: BRUSSELS — EU countries must “do their job” to prevent travelers from being stuck in airport queues over Christmas, Migration Commissioner Magnus Brunner told POLITICO, as he singled out Brussels Airport for the way it has handled the new Entry/Exit System. In an interview, Brunner defended the bloc’s digital border system and blamed its problems on national authorities and airports. “Member states had enough time to prepare themselves for this system. They agreed on the system,” Brunner said. “It's a security issue. It has to work … it's up to the member states to do their job.” Advertisement Advertisement EU countries began rolling out the Entry/Exit System, which records the fingerprints and facial images of non-EU visitors to the Schengen area, a year ago. It has been fully operational at all external Schengen border crossings since April. But it has led to long waits at many airports — particularly over the summer, when some countries switched it off during peak periods . Delays persist at some airports, including at Brussels Zaventem, where travelers were forced to wait in lines for up to five hours last month . “Some member states are a bit behind,” Brunner acknowledged. “We have some challenges, like Zaventem for instance, in Belgium, but also in other member states. And they have to do their job. They agreed on the new system, and now it's up to the member states to do their job.” Brunner also said the Commission had offered support from border agency Frontex and funding to help countries implement the system, adding that he was “very confident” the problems would be ironed out before the next holiday rush. Belgian Interior Minister Bernard Quintin pushed back at Brunner’s criticism, with a spokesperson saying his responsibility was to ensure there were enough police officers to staff the infrastructure provided by Brussels Airport Company. The police have “been fully staffing the 12 positions at arrivals,” the spokesperson said, but the airport can process only 500 to 600 non-Schengen passengers an hour, compared with nearly 3,500 who may arrive between 6 a.m. and 10 a.m. on busy days. The airport's infrastructure “cannot cope” with that demand, the spokesperson said, and the company must “make significant changes.” Advertisement Advertisement Brussels Airport did not directly address the criticism from Brunner or Quintin, instead saying in a statement that “all parties involved” were working to fix the delays, including testing new e-gates and pre-registration kiosks, and training more police. "The need for additional infrastructure is also being assessed," the statement said. The Entry/Exit System has logged almost 230 million entries and exits across roughly 1,500 border points, Brunner said. Authorities have refused entry to about 80,000 people, including 2,000 considered security threats because of links to activity such as terrorism or organized crime. “So you see, it actually works. And it pays off,” the Austrian commissioner said. “This is the most modern border management system in the world,” he added. “We have the comparison to the U.S., to Canada, to others, and they're all jealous.” Ceuta stress test As the EU’s migration commissioner, Brunner also faced another major test over the summer, when tens of thousands of people crossed from Morocco into Spain’s North African exclave of Ceuta. The crisis remains an ongoing challenge for Spain and the EU. Advertisement Advertisement Madrid initially said almost all those who crossed from Morocco had returned within days. But thousands remained in Ceuta . More than 3,000 people were living at Trampolín beach when authorities cleared an encampment last week ; more than 1,200 then chose to return voluntarily to Morocco rather than go through the asylum-screening process, according to local authorities. Images of thousands of people swimming toward Ceuta and overwhelming the area quickly became political ammunition , with far-right politicians campaigning for tougher migration policies — turning the crisis into a potent election issue and putting pressure on Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez. Brunner described Ceuta as a warning that the EU needs to be better prepared for sudden arrivals. He recently proposed a plan for cooperation with partner countries, stronger external borders, early-warning systems, and action against smuggling networks. Migration will be a key topic of conversation at this week’s EU leaders’ summit in Brussels. Among the Commission’s plans to tackle migration is a proposal to strengthen Frontex that would see it have a reinforced standing corps of officers able to be deployed more quickly, a bigger role in returning people to non-EU countries, closer cooperation with partner countries and more capacity to monitor the EU’s borders. The Commission has also proposed giving the agency a role in monitoring social media to help spot emerging migration movements. Brunner said the reforms would not mean countries would be forced to host Frontex operations if they did not want them. The plan envisages EU support during border emergencies, but member countries remain responsible for their own external borders. Greece and other countries want the EU to be able to suspend asylum applications during a large influx and Brunner said he is “definitely going ahead” with an emergency response framework, as requested by Commission President Ursula von der Leyen. EU leaders will discuss “concrete steps” at this week's leaders’ summit. Advertisement Advertisement The goal is to make the EU “more flexible” and “more agile” if events like Ceuta occur, where “mass movements are actually engineered and weaponized” against the bloc, he said. Brussels also wants to help partner countries protect their borders to reduce irregular arrivals into Europe. To that end, Brunner on Monday begins a trip to Bangladesh and Pakistan, seeking to strengthen cooperation on migration with the two countries, he said. “We want to help them to protect their borders,” Brunner stated, adding that the EU could support Bangladesh “via Frontex, for instance.” This story has been updated with statements from Interior Minister Bernard Quintin's office and Brussels Airport.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/9/29.text: Listen (2 mins) Save Share Hungary lifts immunity of Prime Minister Magyar, two Orban-era ministers on social media Share Add Al Jazeera on Google Hungary's Prime Minister Peter Magyar speaks during a news conference at the Paks Nuclear Power Plant on July 31, 2026, in Paks, Hungary [Janos Kummer/Getty Images] By AFP and AP Published On 29 Sep 2026 29 Sep 2026 Hungary’s Parliament has stripped Prime Minister Peter Magyar and two ministers in former leader Viktor Orban’s nationalist government of their immunity, clearing the way for prosecutors to pursue separate criminal investigations into each of them. The vote on Monday came after Magyar, who is being investigated for theft, specifically asked for his immunity to be lifted so he could clear himself of “character assassination”. The probes against the Orban-era ministers – who are suspected of embezzlement and bribery – are the first corruption investigations against top government figures from Orban’s 16 years in power. Recommended Stories list of 4 items list 1 of 4 Hungary nominates former Supreme Court chief Andras Baka for presidency list 2 of 4 Hungary elects supreme court judge ousted by Orban as new president list 3 of 4 Heatwave forces nuclear shutdown in Hungary list 4 of 4 Hungary plans to shut down only nuclear power plant amid drought end of list Legislators voted overwhelmingly in favour of lifting their immunity. Orban’s Fidesz party and its ally KDNP boycotted the session. The vote was in response to a request last week from prosecutors seeking to investigate Magyar, as well as former Minister of Culture Balazs Hanko and former Minister of National Development Miklos Sesztak. Magyar is being investigated over an incident at a Budapest nightclub in June 2024, when prosecutors allege he took a mobile phone from a man filming him and threw it into the Danube River. Magyar has called the case a “sham” and last week accused prosecutors of trying “to conflate” the ex-ministers’ cases “with the attempt at political character assassination… which has already failed several times”. Corruption cases Hanko, a legislator from Orban’s Fidesz party, is accused of embezzling more than 40 million euros ($46m) in public funds. Prosecutors allege the money was used to help finance the 2026 parliamentary election campaign and for the personal benefit of others. Advertisement Sesztak, a lawmaker from KDNP, is under investigation over allegedly accepting more than $37.2m in bribes and kickbacks connected to vehicle procurements under Hungary’s state bus company, as well as to state construction projects. Both ministers deny any wrongdoing. The cases come less than six months after Magyar’s Tisza party ended Orban’s 16 years in power with a landslide election victory. Magyar campaigned on pledges to tackle corruption, restore rule-of-law safeguards, and rebuild Hungary’s strained relationship with the European Union. His government has since made fighting alleged corruption and overpriced public procurement a central part of its programme, including plans for a new asset-recovery office focused on wrongdoing linked to the Orban era.

Beállítom Az Európai Bizottság szerda reggel jóváhagyta az utolsó és egyedüliként megmaradt magyar kérelmet a SAFE-hitelre – jelentette be aznap Thomas Regnier, a testület szóvivője Brüsszelben az Euronews kérdésére. A testület tavaly javasolt 150 milliárd eurós közös hitelt védelmi célokra. A SAFE-et az akkori magyar kormány egyedüliként nem szavazta meg az EU miniszteri Tanácsában, a koalíciós pártok országgyűlési határozatban mentek neki, és kommunikációs igazgatójuk, Menczer Tamás kijelentette, hogy „nem kérünk belőle”. Mindezek után az előző kormány beadott egy húszmilliárd eurós előzetes igényt . Helyette csak 16,2 milliárd eurót szántak Magyarországnak, az így is a harmadik legnagyobb szelet lett volna, holtversenyben az EU egyetlen atomhatalmával, Franciaországgal. A biztonság kedvéért az előző kormány még ezt is túligényelte egy 17,4 milliárd eurós tervvel. A terv bonyolultságára és a túligénylésre hivatkozva az Európai Bizottság márciusra már csak a magyar tervet nem hagyta jóvá . A testület jelezte, hogy a kérelemre ugyanaz a jogszabály vonatkozna , mint amellyel a tagállami miniszterek részlegesen befagyasztották a felzárkóztatási támogatásokat, ez a SAFE-hitel szerződésének megkötésénél jelenthetett volna gondot. (Azt az eljárást néhány hete fejezték be .) Az új kormány szeptemberben 5,4 milliárd euróra mérsékelte az igényelt összeget. A bizottsági zöld jelzés után a tagállami kormányok döntenek a Tanácsban. Elvben egy hónapjuk van erre, ráadásul utána még magát a hitelszerződést is meg kell kötni. A hitellel jár majd egy előleg is. Regnier szerdán azt is elmondta, hogy összesen több mint 21 milliárd euró maradt a 150-ből, emiatt várhatóan felveszik a kapcsolatot a tagállami kormánnyal.
